{{Short description|American physicist (born 1937)}}
'''Maury Tigner''' (born 22 April 1937) is an American [[physicist]] working on [[particle accelerators]] and experimental [[particle physics]].

Tigner studied physics at the [[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute]] until 1958 and received a PhD degree from [[Cornell University]] in 1964. He stayed there and became a professor of physics from 1977 to 1994. After a stay at [[DESY]], he led the development and construction of the [[Cornell Electron Storage Ring]], which started operation in 1979.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://cerncourier.com/a/cornells-laboratory-is-at-the-crossroads/|title=Cornell’s laboratory is at the crossroads|publisher=CERN|access-date=30 October 2022}}</ref> From 1994 to 2000 Tigner worked at the [[Institute of High Energy Physics]] of the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]] in Beijing, contributing to the development of [[Beijing Electron–Positron Collider II|BEPC II]]. In 2000, he moved back to Cornell, leading the laboratory of elementary particle physics until 2006.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11610013.html|title=M. Tigner|publisher=AIP|access-date=30 October 2022}}</ref>

Tigner played a major role in the development of the [[Superconducting Super Collider]], leading the Central Design Group at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] formed in 1984,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hep.net/ssc/new/history/appendixa.html |title= The Superconducting Super Collider Project. A Summary |author=HEPAP's Subpanel on Vision for the Future of High-Energy Physics |date=May 1994 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080708200756/http://www.hep.net/ssc/new/history/appendixa.html |archive-date=8 July 2008}}</ref> and worked on development of the [[International Linear Collider]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.symmetrymagazine.org/article/junejuly-2007/industry-eyes-the-next-big-collider|title=Industry eyes the next big collider|date=1 July 2007|access-date=30 October 2022}}</ref>

Tigner became a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1991<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amacad.org/person/maury-tigner|title=Maury Tigner|access-date=30 October 2022}}</ref> and a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1993.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/maury-tigner-q1abaj/ |title=Member Directory |publisher=National Academy of Sciences |access-date=30 October 2022}}</ref> He received the [[Robert R. Wilson Prize]] in 2000<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?first_nm=Maury&last_nm=Tigner&year=2000 |title=2000 Robert R. Wilson Prize for Achievement in the Physics of Particle Accelerators Recipient: Maury Tigner |publisher=APS |quote=For notable contributions to the accelerator field as an inventor, designer, builder, and leader, including early pioneering developments in superconducting radio-frequency systems, inspiration and intellectual leadership for the construction of CESR, and leadership of the SSC Central Design Group |access-date=30 October 2022}}</ref> and the [[Leo Szilard Lectureship Award]] of the [[American Physical Society]] in 2005.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Tigner&first_nm=Maury&year=2005 |title=2005 Leo Szilard Lectureship Award Recipient|publisher=APS|access-date=30 October 2022}}</ref>
